Verse 37:4: ﴿Indeed, your God is One.﴾ It is said: this is the answer to their saying, "Has he made the gods into one god?"

(p-117) ﴿Lord of the heavens and the earth﴾: this is a predicate following another predicate, or the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "He is the Lord."

﴿And of what is between them, and Lord of the easts﴾: that is, the places where the sun rises. There are three hundred and sixty rising-points, and likewise the setting-points; it rises each day at one of them and sets at one of them, and it does not rise or set at the same point two days running. As for ﴿Lord of the two easts and Lord of the two wests﴾ [al-Rahman: 17], it means the rising-points and setting-points of summer and winter. As for "Lord of the East and the West," it means the direction: the East is a direction and the West is a direction.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 37, verse 6:

﴿Indeed, We have adorned the nearest heaven﴾ — al-Qurbā minkum (the nearer to you); it is the feminine of al-Adnā (the nearest).

﴿with an adornment, the stars﴾ — Ḥamzah and Ḥafṣ (read it as such), in apposition (badal) to "adornment" (al-zīnah). The meaning is: "Indeed, We have adorned the nearest heaven with the stars." "Bi-zīnatin al-kawākiba" — Abū Bakr (read it with the accusative), in apposition (badal) to the place (maḥall) of "bi-zīnatin", or by supposing an implied "a'nī" (I mean), or by making the verbal noun (maṣdar) operate on its object in the indefinite (tanwīn) form, "bi-zīnatin al-kawākiba". Others (read it) "bi-zīnati al-kawākibi", with the verbal noun annexed (iḍāfah) to its agent (fā'il), meaning: by the stars having adorned it; its original form being "bi-zīnatin al-kawākibu". Or by annexing it to its object (maf'ūl), meaning: by God having adorned the stars and made them beautiful, because they only adorned the heaven on account of their own beauty in themselves; its original form being "bi-zīnatin al-kawākiba", according to the reading of Abū Bakr.

﴿And as a guard﴾ is construed according to sense (*ḥaml ʿalā al-maʿnā*, a grammatical principle of agreeing a word with its intended meaning rather than its form), because the meaning is: "Indeed We created the stars as an adornment for the heaven and as a guard against the devils." This is like His saying: ﴿And We have certainly adorned the nearest heaven with lamps, and made them missiles against the devils﴾ [al-Mulk: 5]. Or the causal verb is implied, as if it were said: "And as a guard from every devil, We adorned it with the stars." Or its meaning is: "We guarded it with a guarding."

﴿from every rebellious devil﴾, one who has departed from obedience. And the pronoun in

﴿They cannot listen﴾, for every devil, because it carries the sense of "the devils," so "yassamma'ūn" (with the sād-doubled form) is read by the Kufan (a reader from Kufa) other than Abu Bakr. Its original form is "yatasamma'ūn," and "al-tasamma'" (eavesdropping, seeking to hear) means seeking to hear. It is said: "He eavesdropped (tasamma'a), so he heard," or "so he did not hear." It should be a separate, new sentence, beginning a narrative of the condition of those who steal hearing, and that they cannot listen to the speech of the angels, or eavesdrop. It has also been said: its original form is "li'allā yasma'ū" (so that they do not hear), the lām was deleted as it was deleted in "ji'tuka an tukrimanī" (I came to you that you might honour me), so "allā yassamma'ū" remained, then "an" was deleted and its governing effect was nullified, as in his saying: [p. 118]

> Ala ayyuhā al-zājirī ihḍur al-waghā…

This (explanation) is strained, and the Qur'an must be protected from the like of it, for each of the two particles is not rejected on its own, but their combination is objectionable. The difference between "sami'tu fulānan yataḥaddathu" (I heard so-and-so speaking), "sami'tu ilayhi yataḥaddathu" (I listened to him speaking), "sami'tu ḥadīthahu" (I heard his speech), and "ilā ḥadīthihi" (to his speech) is that the verb transitive by itself conveys perception, while the verb transitive by "ilā" conveys listening together with perception.

﴿to the exalted assembly﴾, that is, the angels, because they dwell in the heavens. The humans and the jinn are the "lower assembly," because they are the inhabitants of the earth.

﴿and they are pelted﴾, they are struck with shooting stars,

﴿from every side﴾, from all the directions of the heaven, from whatever direction they ascend for the purpose of stealing hearing.

{Duhuran} is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), meaning: they are hurled for the sake of repelling (duhur), which is expulsion (al-tard); or it is a circumstantial state (hal), meaning: they are repelled (madhhurin); or because hurling and expulsion are close in meaning, so it is as if it were said: they are driven away (yudhharun), or [it is] a hurling (qadhfan).

{And for them is a punishment perpetual}, lasting, from "al-wusub", meaning: in this world they are pelted with shooting stars, and in the Hereafter there has been prepared for them a kind of punishment that is lasting and unceasing.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 37, verse 10:

"Except one who snatches a snatch" (إلا مَن): in the place of nominative case (raf'), it is a substitute (badal) for the waw in "they do not listen" (لا يَسَّمَّعُونَ). That is: the devils do not listen, except the devil who ﴿snatched the snatch﴾, i.e., plundered the plunder, meaning he took something of their speech swiftly.

﴿So a flaming fire pursued him﴾: it overtook him.

﴿Flaming fire﴾: i.e., a meteor of stoning.

﴿Piercing﴾: shining.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 37, verse 11:

﴿So ask them﴾: that is, ask the disbelievers of Makkah (fastaftihim, "ask for a ruling/inquire of them").

﴿Are they stronger in creation?﴾ That is: more powerful in creation, from their saying "shadid al-khalq" ("strong in creation") and "fi khalqihi shiddah" ("in his creation there is strength"). Or it means "more difficult and harder to create," in the sense of a refutation of their denial of resurrection: whoever finds it easy to create these great creatures, and for whom their bringing into being is not hard, for him the creation of humankind is easier.

﴿Or those whom We have created﴾: he intends what was mentioned of His creation, namely the angels, the heavens, the earth, and what is between them. "Man" (man) is used here, as a dominance of rational beings over others (taghlib li-l-ʿuqala ʿala ghayrihim), and the reading of those who read "am man ʿadadna" (with tashdid and takhfif, i.e., ʿaddadna and ʿadadna) points to this.

﴿Indeed We created them from clay, sticky clay﴾: lasib, that is, adhering, or lazim (clinging). It was also read with this meaning. This is a testimony against them of weakness, because what is made of clay is not described as hard or strong. Or it is an argument against them: the sticky clay from which they were created is dust, so from where do they find it strange that they should be created from dust like it? Hence they said: "When we are dust..." And this meaning is supported by what follows of the mention of their denial of resurrection.

(Verse 12) ﴿Nay, you wonder﴾ at their denying you,

﴿while they mock﴾: they mock you and your wonder; or, you wonder at their denial of the Resurrection while they mock the matter of the Resurrection. "Bal 'ajibtu" (بَلْ عَجِبْتُ) is read by Hamza and 'Ali (with a ḍamma on the tāʾ, as first-person speech), meaning: I have deemed it great (istaʿẓamtu). Al-ʿajab (الْعَجَب) is a sense of awe that comes over a person when he regards something as great; it is applied in the sense of magnification with respect to Him (Exalted), because He is not subject to such awe. Or its meaning is: "Say, O Muhammad: Nay, I wonder."

Translation:

﴿And when they are reminded, they do not remember﴾, and their habit is that whenever they are admonished with something, they do not take admonition from it.

Translation of the passage:

﴿And when they see a sign﴾, a miracle, such as the splitting of the moon, and the like,

﴿they mock﴾ (yastaskhirūn): some of them call upon one another to mock at it, or they exaggerate in mockery.

﴿And they say, "This is"﴾, meaning: what is this?

﴿"nothing but clear magic"﴾, meaning: evident.

﴿أإذا﴾, an interrogative of denial (istifham inkar),

﴿when we have died and become dust and bones, shall we indeed be resurrected?﴾ That is: Will we be raised up when we have become dust and bones?!

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 37, verse 17:

﴿Or our forefathers?﴾ It is in the grammatical position of coordination (ma'tuf) with the locative position (mahall) of "inna" and its noun, or with the pronoun in "mab'uthun" (resurrected). The meaning is: "Will our forefathers also be resurrected?!" This is for the sake of greater disbelief, meaning that they are more ancient, so their resurrection is even more remote and more false. "Aw ababuna" (or our forefathers), with a sukun on the waw, is the reading of Madani and Shami, meaning: "Will one of us be resurrected?!" This is for the sake of exaggerating the denial.

﴿The ancients﴾: the most ancient ones.

Say: "Yes" (نَعَمْ), and you will be resurrected (تُبْعَثُونَ). "نِعَمْ" and "عَلِيٌّ," and they are two dialects (لُغَتانِ).

﴿And you will be humbled﴾ (وَأنْتُمْ داخِرُونَ): abased (صاغِرُونَ).

(p-120) ﴿Fa-innamā﴾ (so indeed) is the answer to an implied conditional clause, whose sense is: "If it is so, then there is not ﴿hiya﴾ (it) except ﴿zajratun wāḥidatun﴾ (one single shout)." The pronoun ﴿hiya﴾ does not refer back to anything; it is ambiguous (mubham), and its clarification (mūḍiḥuhā) is its predicate, ﴿zajratun wāḥidatun﴾. It is also permissible to read it as: "Indeed, the resurrection (al-ba'tha) is one single shout," and this second shout is the second blast (al-nafkhah al-thāniyah). Al-zajrah (the shout) means a loud cry, from your saying, "The herdsman shouted at (zajara) the camels or the sheep," when he cried out at them.

﴿Fa-idhā hum﴾ (then, behold, they are), alive and seeing (buṣarā'),

﴿yanẓurūna﴾ (looking) at the evil of their deeds, or waiting (yantaẓirūna) for what is about to befall them.

**"And they will say, 'Woe to us! This is the Day of Recompense.'"** (Qur'an 37:20)

Al-Wayl (woe): a word that the speaker utters at the time of ruin and destruction.

"This is the Day of Recompense" (hadha yawmu al-din): that is, the day on which we will be judged (nudan), meaning we will be repaid for our deeds.

This is the day of Decision (al-Fasl), the day of judgment and of distinguishing between the groups of guidance and misguidance,

﴿the Day of Decision, which you used to deny.﴾ Then it is possible that ﴿This is the Day of Religion﴾ [al-Saffat: 20] up to His words ﴿Gather them﴾ [al-Saffat: 22] is part of the speech of the disbelievers among themselves; and it is possible that it is part of the speech of the angels to them; and it is possible that ﴿Woe to us! This is the Day of Religion﴾ [al-Saffat: 20] is part of the speech of the disbelievers, and "This is the Day of Decision" is part of the speech of the angels, as a reply to them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 37, verse 22:

﴿Assemble﴾, the address of Allah to the angels,

﴿those who did wrong﴾, i.e., disbelieved,

﴿and their spouses﴾, i.e., their counterparts (ashbahahum) and their companions (qurana'uhum) among the devils (shayatin), or their disbelieving women (nisa'ahum al-kafirat). The waw (wa) is in the sense of "with" (ma'a). It has also been said that it is for conjunction (li-l-'atf). It was also read in the nominative (bi-l-raf'), as a conjunction (ataf) upon the pronoun in "dhalamu" (zalamu, "they did wrong"),

﴿and what they used to worship﴾.

"from besides Allah," that is, the idols,

"then guide them," point them out [to the way]. From al-Asma'i: "hadaytuhu fi al-din hudan" and "fi al-tariq hidayatan" (I guided him in religion, guidance; and on the road, guidance).

"to the path of Hellfire," the way of the Fire.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 37, verse 24:**

﴿Stop them﴾, i.e., detain them.

﴿Indeed they are to be questioned﴾, about their statements and their actions.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 37, verse 25:

﴿What is the matter with you that you do not help one another?﴾ That is: none of you helps another. This is a rebuke to them for their inability to help one another, after they used to help one another in the world. It was also said: it is a reply to Abu Jahl, when he said on the day of Badr: ﴿We are a united body that will prevail﴾ [al-Qamar: 44]. The phrase ﴿مَا لَكُمْ﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: "What is the matter with you, not helping one another?"

(p-121) ﴿Nay, today they are submitting﴾: obedient and yielding. Or, they have surrendered to one another, and each has forsaken the other out of helplessness, so all of them are submitting, none of them victorious.

And they turn to one another, questioning one another (﴿وَأقْبَلَ بَعْضُهم عَلى بَعْضٍ﴾): that is, the follower turns to the one who was followed.

﴿يَتَساءَلُونَ﴾: they dispute with one another.

They said, that is, the followers to those they followed: "Indeed you used to come to us from the right," meaning from strength and coercion, since the right hand is described as strong, and it is by it that the seizing is done. That is, you used to drive us to misguidance and compel us to it.

﴿They said﴾, that is, the leaders:

﴿"Rather, you were not believers"﴾. That is, rather, you yourselves refused faith and turned away from it, though you were able to attain it, choosing disbelief over it, not being compelled.

Qur'anic quotations in ﴿ ﴾ are rendered with their meaning.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 37, verse 30:

﴿And We had no authority over you﴾: a domination by which We would strip you of your capacity and your choice.

﴿Rather, you were a people overstepping the bounds﴾: rather, you were a people who chose transgression (tughyan) of your own accord.

﴿So the word of our Lord has come true against us﴾: that is, it became binding on us all.

﴿"Indeed we are going to taste (the punishment)"﴾: that is, the threat of Allah, that we will certainly taste His punishment, without doubt, because of His knowledge of our state. Had he related the threat exactly as it was, he would have said, "Indeed you are going to taste (it)," but he shifted it to the first-person speaker form, because they are speaking this about themselves. A similar example is his saying:

"Hawazin has claimed that my wealth is little..."

Had he related her words exactly, he would have said, "your wealth is little."

﴿So we led you astray﴾, meaning we called you to error (al-ghayy),

﴿for indeed we were ourselves astray﴾, meaning we intended to lead you astray, so that you would become like us.
(p-122) ﴿Indeed, We do thus with the criminals﴾ — i.e., with the polytheists. Indeed, We do the like of that deed with every criminal.

﴿Indeed, when it was said to them, "There is no deity except Allah," they would be arrogant,﴾ Indeed they, when they heard the word of tawhid (the affirmation of God's oneness), became arrogant and refused anything but shirk (associating partners with God).

﴿And they say, "Are we really going to abandon our gods for a mad poet?"﴾

Read with two hamzas, "أإنّا" (*ʾa-ʾinnā*), as "Shami" (the reading of the Syrian school) and "Kufi" (the reading of the Kufan school).

Here "they" refers to the disbelievers, and "a mad poet" refers to Muhammad (ﷺ).
﴿And you will not be recompensed except for what you used to do﴾, without any increase.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 37, verse 40:

﴿Except the chosen servants of Allah﴾, with the lam pronounced with a fatha, read by "the Kufans and the Madinans," and likewise what follows it, meaning: "but the servants of Allah," as an exception that is disconnected (istithna' munqati', an exception in which the excluded item is not of the same category as what precedes it).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 37, verses 41–42:

﴿For them is a known provision﴾ ﴿fruits﴾. He explains the known provision as fruits, which are whatever is enjoyed and not eaten as sustenance for preserving health. The meaning is that all their provision is fruits, because they are free from needing staple foods to preserve their health, since their bodies are perfectly constructed and created for eternity. So what they eat is for pleasure. It is also possible that what is meant is: "a known provision described by qualities for which it was created, of good taste, fragrance, delight and beautiful appearance." It was also said: it is known in its time, like His saying: ﴿And for them is their provision therein, morning and evening﴾ [Maryam: 62]. And the soul is more at rest with this (view),

﴿And they are honoured﴾: made luxurious (mu'annamun).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 37, verses 41–42:

﴿For them is a known provision﴾ ﴿fruits﴾. He explains the known provision as fruits, which are whatever is enjoyed and not eaten as sustenance for preserving health. The meaning is that all their provision is fruits, because they are free from needing staple foods to preserve their health, since their bodies are perfectly constructed and created for eternity. So what they eat is for pleasure. It is also possible that what is meant is: "a known provision described by qualities for which it was created, of good taste, fragrance, delight and beautiful appearance." It was also said: it is known in its time, like His saying: ﴿And for them is their provision therein, morning and evening﴾ [Maryam: 62]. And the soul is more at rest with this (view),

﴿And they are honoured﴾: made luxurious (mu'annamun).
in the Gardens of Bliss, it may be a circumstantial adverbial (ẓarf), and it may be a state (ḥāl), and it may be a second predicate (khabar) after a predicate, and likewise:

on thrones, facing one another.

Note: The page marker "(p-١٢٣)" is omitted from the translation.

Translation:

﴿On thrones, facing one another.﴾ Facing one another is more complete for joy, and more intimate.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 37, verse 45:

﴿They are served with a cup﴾, without a hamza, according to Abu 'Amr and Hamzah in pause, while the others read it with a hamza. A cup (ka's) is said of the glass in which there is wine, and wine itself is also called "ka's." It is reported from al-Akhfash: every "ka's" in the Qur'an refers to wine. Likewise in the tafsir of Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father,

﴿from a flowing spring﴾, that is, from a flowing drink, or from a flowing river, which is that which runs on the surface of the earth and is visible to the eyes. It is described with what water is described with, because it flows in Paradise in rivers, just as water flows. Allah (Exalted) says: ﴿And rivers of wine﴾ [Muhammad: 15].

[Surah 37, verse 46]

﴿Bayḍāʾ﴾ (white): an adjective of the cup (kaʾs).

﴿Ladhdhah﴾ (delight): it is described as delight, as though it were the very essence of delight and its embodiment; or [it means] "possessing delight."

﴿Lil-shāribīn﴾: for those who drink.

﴿There is no intoxication (ghawl) in it﴾: i.e., it does not dull their minds (lā taghtālu ʿuqūlahum) as the wines of this world do. It derives from "ghālahu, yaghūluhu, ghawlan," meaning when it destroys him and corrupts him.

﴿Nor will they be drained by it﴾: i.e., they will not become drunk. It derives from "nazafa al-shārib," meaning when the drinker's intellect departs. The intoxicated person is called "nazīf" and "manzūf." "Yunzifūn" is the reading of ʿAlī and Ḥamzah, meaning: they will not become drunk; or, their drink will not drain (lā yanzifu sharābuhum), from "anzafa al-shārib," meaning when his intellect or his drink departs.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 37, verse 48:

﴿And with them are those restraining their glances, [and] large-eyed,﴾ — they have restrained their eyes upon their husbands, not extending their glance toward others.

﴿Large-eyed (ʿīn)﴾ — the plural of ʿaynāʾ, that is, having large, wide eyes (najlāʾ, wāsiʿat al-ʿayn).

"As if they were a hidden egg" (﴿كَأَنَّهُنَّ بَيْضٌ مَكْنُونٌ﴾)—protected, guarded. He likened them to ostrich eggs, hidden away, in their clarity and purity (ṣafāʾ). The Arabs liken women to these, and call them "bayḍāt al-khudūr" (the eggs of the curtained chambers). And it is joined by conjunction (ʿuṭifa).

﴿So some of them turned to others, asking one another.﴾ He means the people of Paradise.

﴿Asking one another.﴾ "On (p-124)" "They are passed around among them" (Qur'an 37:45). The meaning is: "They drink and converse over the wine, as is the custom of drinkers." He said:

*Nothing remained of pleasures except*
*the talk of the noble over wine.*

So some of them turn to others, asking one another about what happened to them and to those (who were) against them in the world. Except that it was expressed in the past tense, as is known in its reports.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 37, verse 52:

﴿يَقُولُ أإنَّكَ﴾ — with two hamzas (ʾa-ʾinnaka), according to the Syrian and Kufan readers —

﴿لَمِنَ المُصَدِّقِينَ﴾ — "Lamina al-musaddiqin" is rendered: "Are you truly among those who affirm?" — [referring to] the Day of Judgement.

Translation of the Qur'anic text:
﴿He says: "Are you truly among those who affirm [the Day of Judgement]?"﴾

﴿When we have died and become dust and bones, shall we indeed be recompensed?﴾ [It means] "we will be recompensed" (*lamajziyyun*), derived from *al-dayn* (الدَّيْنُ), which means recompense (*al-jaza'*).

Says that speaker (the one speaking): "Would you like to look down (into the Fire)?" — toward the Fire, so that I may show you that companion.

It is said: in Paradise there are openings (kuwan, sing. kuwwa), through which its people look out upon the people of the Fire. Or God (Exalted) said to the people of Paradise: "Would you like to look down into the Fire, so that you may know where your station is relative to the station of the people of the Fire?"

[The Muslim] looks (fa-ṭṭala'a), [and sees him]: "﴿So he looked﴾," the believer (al-muslim).

"﴿and saw him﴾," that is, his companion (qarīnahu).

"﴿in the midst of the Blazing Fire﴾," in its middle (wasaṭihā).

Translation:

﴿He said: "By God, you nearly brought me to ruin."﴾ "In" (إنْ) is a lightened form of the heavy (إنّ, mukhaffafah min al-thaqilah), and it enters upon "kada" (كادَ, to be about to / nearly), just as it enters upon "kana" (كانَ, to be). The lam (اللامُ) is the one that distinguishes it from the negative (النافِيَةِ, al-nafiyah). "Al-irda'" (الإرداءُ) means al-ihlak (الإهلاكُ, destruction). And with the ya' (بِالياءِ), in both cases, Ya'qub (يَعْقُوبُ) [is read: "li-turdiyanni"].

﴿Had it not been for the grace of my Lord﴾, which is ʿiṣmah (divine protection from sin) and tawfiq (divine enablement) in holding fast to the handhold of Islam,

﴿I would certainly have been among those brought forth﴾, among those who are brought forth to the punishment, just as you and those like you were brought forth to it.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 37, verses 58–59:

﴿Are we not to die﴾ ﴿except for our first death? And we will not be punished﴾. The fa' (al-fa') here is for conjunction (li-l-'atf) with something omitted (ma'huf), its implied sense being: "Are we not to be immortal and blessed, so that we are not to die" ﴿(p-125)﴾ "and not to be punished?!" The meaning is that this is the condition of the believers: that they will taste only the first death, unlike the disbelievers, who wish for death every hour. It was said to a wise man (Hakim): "What is worse than death?" He said: "That in which death is wished for." This is a statement that the believer makes, speaking of the blessing of God, in the hearing of his companion, so that it becomes a rebuke to him and an increase in his punishment. "Mawtatana" is in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar), and the exception (al-istithna') is connected (muttasil), its implied sense being: "And we do not die except once." Or it is disconnected (munqati'), and its implied sense being: "But the first death has already occurred in this world." Then he said to his companion, rebuking him:

Translation:

﴿Indeed, this﴾ — i.e., the matter in which we are —

﴿is truly the great triumph﴾. Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said:
﴿For the like of this let the workers work.﴾ It is also said that this is from his own words.

ذَلِكَ خَيْرٌ نُزُلًا، تَمْيِيزٌ

Translation:

﴿Is that better as an entertainment (nuzul)﴾ — a tamyiz (specification of comparison).

﴿Or the tree of zaqqum?﴾ That is: the delights of Paradise, and what is in it of pleasures, food and drink, are better as an entertainment; or is the tree of zaqqum better as an entertainment?! And "nuzul" (nuzul, provision prepared for a guest): what is provided for the one who arrives at a place of sustenance; and "zaqqum" (zaqqum): a bitter tree that grows in Tihama.

"Indeed, We made it a trial for the wrongdoers." (It is) a test (miḥnah) and a punishment for them in the Hereafter, or a trial for them in this world. That is because they said: "How can there be a tree in the Fire, when the Fire burns trees?!" So they were denied.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 37, verse 64:

﴿Indeed, it is a tree that springs forth from the root of Hellfire.﴾ It is said: its place of growth is at the bottom of Jahannam (Hell), and its branches rise up to its levels (darakat).

Its spathe (ṭalʿ) is like the heads of devils (ru'ūs al-shayāṭīn).

"Al-ṭalʿ" is for the date palm, and it was borrowed for what emerges from the zaqqum tree from its fruit-bearing. It is compared to the heads of devils to indicate its extreme loathsomeness and ugliness of appearance, because the devil is hated and detested in people's natures, since they believe it to be pure evil. It was also said: "al-shayṭān" is a bitter plant (ḥabba ʿarfāʾ), ugly in appearance and extremely frightful.

﴿Indeed they will be eating from it﴾, from the tree, that is, from its spathe (ṭalʿ),

﴿and filling their bellies with it﴾, filling their bellies, because of the severe hunger that will overcome them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 37, verse 67:

﴿Then indeed for them over it﴾, over their eating (of it),

﴿a mixture﴾, a blending and a mixing,

﴿of boiling water﴾, hot water, which scalds their faces and cuts up their intestines, just as He said - describing the drink of the people of Paradise -: ﴿and its mixture is from Tasnim﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 27]. The meaning: then indeed they fill their bellies from the tree of al-Zaqqum, and it is hot, burning their bellies and making them thirsty, so they are not given to drink except after a long delay, as a punishment for them through that thirst. Then they are given to drink what is even hotter, namely the drink mixed with boiling water (ḥamīm).

Then indeed their return is to the Hellfire (﴿ثُمَّ إنَّ مَرْجِعَهم لإلى الجَحِيمِ﴾). That is: they are taken away from their stations and dwellings in the Hellfire, which are the levels (al-darakat) in which they were made to dwell, to the tree of al-Zaqqum. So they eat from it until they are filled, and after that they are given drink, then they are returned to their levels. The sense of delay (al-tarakhi) in this is clear.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 37, verses 69–70:

﴿Indeed, they found their fathers astray,﴾ ﴿so they were rushing in their footsteps.﴾ He gives as the reason for their deserving to fall into those hardships their blind imitation (taqlid) of their fathers in the religion, their following them in error, and their abandoning the pursuit of evidence (dalil). "Al-ihra' (الإهراع)" means intense haste (al-israa al-shadid), as if they were being driven on (yuhathhathuna hathth-an).

﴿أكْثَرُ الأوَّلِينَ﴾ — meaning the past nations (الأُمَمَ الخالِيَةَ) — by blind imitation (التَقْلِيدِ) and by abandoning reflection and contemplation (وتَرْكِ النَظَرِ والتَأمُّلِ).
﴿And We had certainly sent among them warners.﴾ [They were] prophets, who warned them of the consequences.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 37, verse 73:

﴿So look how was the end of those who were warned﴾ i.e., those who were warned and admonished, that is, they were all destroyed.

Except the servants of God who were sincere (﴿إلا عِبادَ اللهِ المُخْلَصِينَ﴾). That is: except those among them who believed and made their religion sincerely for God, or whom God made sincere for His religion, according to the two readings.

And when he mentioned the sending of warners to the earlier nations and the evil end of those who were warned, He followed that with the mention of Noah and his supplication, when he despaired of his people, by His saying: ﴿And Noah certainly called out to Us﴾, meaning he called upon Us to save him from drowning. It was also said that what is meant is his saying: ﴿I am overcome, so help [me]﴾ [al-Qamar: 10]. ﴿So how excellent were the Responders!﴾ The lam that enters upon "ni'ma" (how excellent) is the lam of an oath that is elided in the sentence, and the one specified for praise is omitted; its estimated form is: "And Noah certainly called out to Us, so by God, how excellent were We as Responders!" The use of the plural indicates majesty and greatness. The meaning is: We answered him in the finest manner, helped him against his enemies, and took vengeance upon them in the most emphatic way.

﴿And We delivered him and his family﴾, and those who believed with him, and his children,

﴿from the great distress﴾, which was drowning.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 37, verse 77:

﴿And We made his descendants the survivors﴾, while others had perished. ﴿Peace be upon Nuh﴾. That is, they greet him with a greeting (*taslim*), and they invoke blessings upon him. This is *al-kalam al-mahki* (quoted speech), like your saying: "I read *(sūratun anzalnāhā)*," where the words in parentheses are quoted verbatim, and the phrase *sūratun anzalnāhā* ("a sura that We sent down") is presented as the quoted words themselves.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 37, verse 84: ﴿When he came to his Lord with a sound heart﴾. "Idh" (when) is connected to what is implied in al-shi'a (the party, the followers) of the sense of mushaya'a (following, supporting), meaning: "And indeed, among those who followed him in his religion and his piety, at the time he came to his Lord with a heart sound from shirk (associating partners with God), or from the afflictions of the hearts, was Abraham." Or it is connected to an elided verb, which is: "Remember" (udhkur). The meaning of the heart's coming to its Lord is that he sincerely devoted his heart to God, and God knew this about him, so He used "coming" as a figure of speech for that.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 37, verse 85:

﴿إذْ﴾ is a *badal* (a substitute or apposition, grammatically replacing the word it follows) of the first [﴿إذ﴾ in the previous verse].

﴿قالَ لأبِيهِ وقَوْمِهِ ماذا تَعْبُدُونَ﴾ ("When he said to his father and his people: 'What is it that you worship?'")

Qur'anic quotation: ﴿Is it a falsehood, gods other than God, that you desire?﴾ "Ifkan" is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), its underlying sense being: "Do you desire gods other than God as a falsehood?!" The object was placed before the verb for emphasis (al-'inaya), and the object of purpose was placed before the direct object because it was more important to him that he confront them with the fact that they were in falsehood and vanity in their polytheism. It is also permissible for "ifkan" to be a direct object (maf'ul bihi), meaning: "Do you desire a falsehood?!" Then he explained the falsehood by his words "gods other than God," either as being a falsehood in itself, or as a circumstantial state (hal), meaning: "Do you desire gods other than God being liars?!"

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 37, verse 87:

﴿So what is your opinion﴾, i.e., what is your thought (ẓann) ﴿concerning the Lord of the worlds﴾, while you worship other than Him? And "mā" (what) is in the nominative case by being the subject (mubtada'), and the predicate (khabar) is "ẓannukum" (your thought). Or: "So what is your thought about Him? What will He do to you?! And how will He punish you, when you have worshipped other than Him, and you know that He is the true Bestower of blessings, so He is truly deserving of worship?!"

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 37, verse 88:

﴿So he cast a glance at the stars﴾ That is: he looked at the stars, casting his sight up toward the sky, pondering within himself how he might contrive [an excuse]. Or [it means] he showed them that he was looking at the stars, because they believed in the science of the stars (ʿilm al-nujum, the knowledge of astrology), so he gave them the impression that he had inferred from a sign that he would fall ill.

**Fa-qala innī saqīm** (﴿So he said, "Indeed, I am ill."﴾) means: I am about to become sick (mushārif li-l-suqm), and the sickness was the plague (ṭā'ūn). This was the most prevalent of their diseases, and they feared contagion (al-'adwā), so that they would separate from him. They fled from him to their festival, and left him in the house of the idols, with no one with him. So he did to the idols what he did. They said: "The knowledge of the stars was true; then the occupation with knowing it was abrogated (naskh)." Lying is forbidden except by allusion (ta'ríd). What Abraham (peace be upon him) said was an equivocal statement (mi'rād min al-kalām), meaning: "I will fall sick," or "one who has death at his neck is sick." From this comes the proverb: "Safety is a sickness enough." A man died suddenly, and they said: "He died while healthy," whereupon a Bedouin said: "Is one healthy when death is at his neck?!" Or he intended: "I am sick in soul because of your disbelief," as one says: "I am sick at heart because of such-and-such."

﴿So they turned away﴾, i.e., they withdrew from him,

﴿turning their backs﴾. That is: showing their backs.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 37, verse 91:

﴿Then he turned aside to their gods﴾, he inclined toward them secretly,

﴿and said﴾, mockingly,

﴿"Will you not eat?"﴾, and there was food beside them.

﴿What is wrong with you that you do not speak?﴾ The plural is formed with the waw and nun (the sound masculine plural ending, *tanṭiqūna*), because He addressed them with the form of address used for those who have intellect (*ʿaql*).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 37, verse 93:

﴿So he turned upon them, striking (them)﴾, that is, he came upon them stealthily. It is as if he said: "So he struck them, a striking." This is because "رَاغَ عَلَيْهِمْ" (*rāgha ʿalayhim*, "he turned upon them") carries the meaning of "ضَرَبَهُمْ" (*ḍarabahum*, "he struck them"). Or the sense is: "فَرَاغَ عَلَيْهِمْ يَضْرِبُهُمْ ضَرْبًا" (*fa-rāgha ʿalayhim yaḍribuhum ḍarban*, "he turned upon them, striking them a blow"), that is, "ضَارِبًا" (*ḍāriban*, "striking").

﴿with the right hand﴾, that is, a severe blow, with force. It is so described because the right hand is the stronger and more forceful of the two limbs. Or it means with strength and firmness. Or it means because of the oath that he had earlier sworn, namely his saying: ﴿By God, I will surely plot against your idols﴾ [al-Anbiya: 57].

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 37, verse 94:**

﴿So they came hastening to him﴾, to Ibrahim (Abraham),

﴿hurrying﴾, i.e., rushing, from "al-zafif" (the hastening), which is speeding. "Yuzaffun" is read by Hamza as "yuzaffun" from "azaffa", when one enters into the zafif, "izfafan" (rushing). It is as if some of them saw him breaking them, and some of them did not see him. So whoever saw him came rushing toward him. Then whoever had not seen him came and said to those who had seen him: ﴿Who has done this to our gods? Indeed, he is of the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Anbiya: 59]. They answered him by way of allusion with their saying: ﴿We heard a youth mention them, called Ibrahim﴾ [al-Anbiya: 60]. Then they all said: "We worship them, and you break them!" So he answered them with his saying:
(p-130) ﴿He said, "Do you worship what you carve?"﴾ [By your own hands.]

﴿And Allah created you and what you do.﴾ And He created what you make with your hands, the idols. Or "mā" is a verbal particle (*mā maṣdariyyah*, a particle that turns the following clause into a verbal noun), meaning: He created your actions. This is our proof for the creation of actions, i.e., Allah is the creator of you and the creator of your actions, so why do you worship other than Him?!

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 37, verse 97:

﴿They said: Build for him﴾, i.e., for his sake,

﴿a building﴾, of stone, its length thirty cubits and its breadth twenty cubits,

﴿then throw him into the blazing fire﴾, into the fire, the intense one. It is also said: every fire that is piled one part above another is called "jaḥīm".

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 37, verse 98:

﴿They intended to plot against him,﴾ by casting him into the fire.

﴿So We made them the lowest,﴾ the vanquished at the time of the casting; so he came out of the fire.

﴿He said, "Indeed I am going to my Lord"﴾, to a place to which He commanded me to go,

﴿He will guide me﴾, He will direct me to what is good for me in my religion, will keep me safe, and will grant me success. "سَيَهْدِينِي", in both (readings), "Ya'qub".

"My Lord, grant me [a child] from among the righteous." [Min al-salihin] means "some of the righteous," and he (Abraham) means a child, because the word hibah (grant/gift) has become predominantly used for a child.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 37, verse 101:

﴿So We gave him the good news of a forbearing boy.﴾ The glad tidings contained three things: that the child is a boy, a male; that he will reach the age of discernment (ḥilm), since a young child is not described as forbearing (ḥalīm); and that he will be forbearing (ḥalīm). And what forbearance is greater than his forbearance when his father proposed to him the slaughter, and he said: ﴿You will find me, if God wills, among the patient﴾ [al-Ṣāffāt: 102], and then he submitted to that.

﴿Then, when he reached with him the age of exertion﴾: he reached the point of going about with his father in his affairs and needs. "With him" (*maʿahu*) is not connected to "reached" (*balagha*), because that would require that both of them reached the limit of exertion together. Nor is it connected to "the exertion" (*al-saʿy*), because the complement of a verbal noun (*masdar*) may not precede it. What remains is that it is an explanation (*bayan*), as if he had said: "When he reached the exertion," meaning the limit at which he was able to exert himself. It was said: "With whom?" He said: "With his father." (p-131) At that time he was thirteen years old.

﴿He said: "O my little son"﴾. Ḥafṣ read it, while the rest read it with a kasra on the *yāʾ*.

﴿"Indeed I see in a dream that I am slaughtering you"﴾. It is read with a fatḥa on the *yāʾ* in both places by the Ḥijāzī readers and Abū ʿAmr. He was told in a dream: "Slaughter your son." The dreams of the prophets are revelation, like revelation while awake. He did not say "I saw" (*raʾaytu*) because he saw it repeatedly. It is said that he saw it on the night of the Tarwiyah, as if someone were saying to him: "Indeed God commands you to slaughter this son of yours." When he woke in the morning he deliberated about it from morning until evening: was this dream from God or from Satan? Therefore that day was named "the Day of Tarwiyah" (deliberation). When evening came he saw the same thing, and he knew that it was from God; therefore that day was named "the Day of ʿArafah" (knowing). Then he saw the same thing on the third night, and he resolved to slaughter him, so that day was named "the Day of Naḥr" (slaughter).

﴿"So see what you think"﴾: from "opinion" (*al-raʾy*), by way of consultation, not from sight with the eye. He did not consult him so that he would return to his own opinion and counsel, but in order to know whether he would be distressed or would be patient. "Turī" (you see) is read by ʿAlī and Ḥamzah, meaning: "What do you perceive of your opinion and make known?"

﴿He said: "O my father, do what you are commanded"﴾, that is, what you are commanded to do. It was also read thus.

﴿"You will find me, God willing, among the patient"﴾, in the slaughter. It is narrated that the one to be slaughtered said to his father: "O my father, take hold of my forelock and sit between my shoulders, so that I do not harm you when the blade strikes me, and do not slaughter me while you look at my face, perhaps you would have mercy on me, and set my face toward the ground." It is also narrated: "Slaughter me while I am prostrating, and convey my greetings to my mother, and if you see fit to return my shirt to my mother, then do so, for perhaps that will be easier for her."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 37, verse 103:

﴿When they both submitted﴾: they yielded to the command of Allah and humbled themselves. From Qatada: "This one submitted his son, and this one submitted himself."

﴿And he threw him down upon his forehead﴾: he laid him down on his forehead (jabin), and placed the knife on his throat, but it did not cut. Then he placed the knife on his nape, and the knife turned over. He was called: "O Ibrahim, you have fulfilled the vision." It is narrated that this place is at the rock that is in Mina.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 37, verses 104–105:

﴿Indeed, this is the clear trial﴾: the manifest test in which the sincere (al-mukhlisun) are distinguished from others, or the evident affliction.

﴿And We ransomed him with a tremendous sacrifice﴾: that is, with something to be slaughtered. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "It was the ram that Habil (Abel) offered, and it was accepted from him, and it grazed in Paradise until Isma'il was ransomed with it." He also said: "Had that sacrifice been completed, it would have become a sunnah (established practice), and people would have slaughtered their sons."

﴿Great﴾: huge in body and fat. This is the sunnah in sacrifices (udhiyah). It is also reported that it fled from Ibrahim at the Jamrah (the stoning pillar), so he threw seven pebbles at it until he caught it, and therefore it remained a sunnah in the stoning ritual. It is also reported that when he slaughtered it, Jibril said: "Allahu akbar, Allahu akbar." The one being sacrificed said: "La ilaha illa Allah, wa Allahu akbar." Ibrahim said: "Allahu akbar wa lillahi al-hamd." So this remained a sunnah.

Abu Hanifah, may Allah be pleased with him, cited this verse regarding one who vows to slaughter his son, holding that he is obligated to slaughter a sheep. The more apparent view is that the one sacrificed was Isma'il. This is the opinion of Abu Bakr, Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn 'Umar, and a group of the Tabi'un, may Allah be pleased with them all, based on the saying of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "I am the son of the two sacrificed ones." One of them is his grandfather Isma'il, and the other is his father 'Abdullah. This is because 'Abd al-Muttalib vowed that if his sons reached ten, he would sacrifice his youngest son as an act of drawing near to Allah, and 'Abdullah was the youngest. So he ransomed him with one hundred camels.

Also, the two horns of the ram were hung in the Ka'bah in the hands of the descendants of Isma'il, until the House burned in the time of al-Hajjaj and Ibn al-Zubayr.

It is reported from al-Asma'i that he said: "I asked Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' about the sacrificed one, and he said: 'O Asma'i, where has your intellect gone? When was Ishaq in Makkah? Isma'il was in Makkah, and he it was who built the House with his father, and the place of sacrifice (manhar) is in Makkah.'"

It is reported from 'Ali, Ibn Mas'ud, al-'Abbas, and a group of the Tabi'un, may Allah be pleased with them all, that it was Ishaq. This is supported by the letter of Ya'qub to Yusuf, peace be upon them both: "From Ya'qub, Israel of Allah, son of Ishaq, the sacrificed one of Allah, son of Ibrahim, the friend of Allah."

The phrase "We ransomed him" is used even though the one who ransomed was Ibrahim, peace be upon him, and Allah (Exalted is He) is the One from whom the ransom was sought, because He is the one who commanded the slaughter. Allah (Exalted is He) gave him the ram so that he could ransom with it.

Here there is a difficulty: either what Ibrahim, peace be upon him, did, by laying him on his side and passing the blade over his throat, counts as slaughter or it does not. If it counts as slaughter, then what is the meaning of ransom? Ransom is release from slaughter by a substitute. If it does not count, then what is the meaning of His saying: ﴿You have fulfilled the vision﴾ [al-Saffat: 105]? He would have fulfilled it only if the slaughter had been valid in itself or as a substitute, and it was not valid.

The answer is that he, peace be upon him, exerted his full effort and did what the slaughterer does, but Allah (Exalted is He) brought about what prevented the blade from proceeding into it. This does not detract from Ibrahim's act. Allah gave him the ram so that his slaughter would stand in place of that reality within Isma'il, as a substitute for him. This is not an abrogation (naskh, the cancellation of a ruling by a later revelation) of the ruling, as some have said. Rather, that ruling was established, except that the locus to which it was attached was not made lawful by the ruling in the manner of ransom, without abrogation. This was a trial, so that the ruling of the command would be firmly settled for the one addressed at the end of the matter. Moreover, what was intended in regard to the son was that he should become a sacrifice, with the ruling attributed to him, honored by the ransom that occurred, free from the disgrace of slaughter, tested with patience and striving, until the state of unveiling. Abrogation occurs only after the intended purpose of the command has been firmly established, not before it. And it is called "ransom" (fida') in the Book, not "abrogation" (naskh).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 37, verse 110:

﴿Thus do We reward the doers of good﴾. He did not say "Indeed, We" (inna) here, as He does elsewhere, because it had already occurred in this story, so He dispensed with repeating it, being satisfied with mentioning it once rather than mentioning it a second time.

﴿Indeed, he was among Our believing servants.﴾ ﴿And We gave him the good news of Isaac, a prophet.﴾ "A prophet" is a *hal muqaddara* (an anticipated circumstantial qualifier, *hal*, meaning a state or condition described for the noun) referring back to "Isaac." It is necessary to posit an omitted *mudaf* (a noun governing a genitive in a construct phrase), meaning: "We gave him the good news of the existence of (*wujud*) Isaac as a prophet." That is, [the good news was] that he would come into existence with prophethood anticipated for him. The governing element of the *hal* is therefore the existence (*wujud*), not the good news (*bishara*).

﴿From among the righteous.﴾ This is a second *hal*. Its occurrence is by way of praise, because every prophet must necessarily be among the righteous.

Translation:

﴿And We blessed him and Isaac﴾: that is, We bestowed upon both of them the blessings of religion and of this world. It is also said: "We blessed Abraham in his offspring, and upon Isaac by bringing forth from his loins a thousand prophets, the first of whom was Jacob and the last of whom was Jesus, peace be upon them all." ﴿And of their offspring are those who do good﴾, that is, believers, ﴿and those who clearly wrong themselves﴾, that is, disbelievers, ﴿manifestly﴾, that is, openly. Or: [the one who] does good to people, and [the one who] wrongs his own soul by transgressing the limits of the Sharia.

In this there is a reminder that the good and the wicked do not have their affairs determined by lineage and descent: the righteous may beget the wicked, and the wicked may beget the righteous. This overturns the notion of inherent natures and elements. Also, [this verse shows that] wrongdoing among their descendants did not bring any defect or shortcoming upon the two of them, and that a person is blamed only for his own bad deeds and is punished only for what his hands have committed, not for what came from his origin or his offspring.

﴿And We had certainly bestowed favor﴾, that is, We bestowed blessings,

﴿upon Musa and Harun﴾, with prophethood (*nubuwwa*).

﴿And We delivered them and their people﴾, the Children of Israel, ﴿from the great distress﴾, that is, from the drowning, or from the dominion of Pharaoh and his people and their tyranny (ghashamihim).

"And We helped them" — that is, Musa and Harun, and their people,

"so they were the victors" — over Pharaoh and his people.
And We gave them both the clear Book (al-Kitab al-Mustabin), the one that is eloquent in its exposition (al-Baligh fi bayanihi), and it is the Torah.

﴿And We guided them both to the straight path﴾: the path of the people of Islam. It is "the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour, not of those who have earned anger, nor of those who are astray."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 37, verse 125:

﴿Do you call upon﴾: do you worship,

﴿Ba'l﴾: it is the name of an idol that was made of gold. Its height was twenty cubits, and it had four faces. They were enchanted by it and magnified it, to the extent that they assigned to its service four hundred attendants (sadin), and they made them into prophets. Its site was called "Bakk," and it was compounded and became "Ba'labakk" (Ba'albek), which is in the lands of al-Sham (Greater Syria). It has been said regarding Ilyas (Elias) and al-Khadir (al-Khidr): they are both living. It has also been said that Ilyas is entrusted with the deserts, just as al-Khadir is entrusted with the seas. Al-Hasan (al-Basri) says: Ilyas and al-Khadir have perished, and we do not say, as people say, that they are both alive.

﴿And you forsake the best of creators﴾: and you abandon the worship of God, who is the best of those who determine (creation)?!

**Allah, your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers the first ones** (﴿اللهَ رَبَّكم ورَبَّ آبائِكُمُ الأوَّلِينَ﴾). Read with the accusative (naṣb) on all of it by the "ʿIrāqī" readers (the Iraqi Qur'an reciters) except Abu Bakr and Abu ʿAmr, as a *badal* (substitution, apposition) of "*aḥsana*" (أحسن), and the others read it with the nominative (raf'), as a *mubtadaʾ* (inchoative, the subject of a nominal sentence).

This is like their saying "al-Khubaybun," meaning Abu Khubayb, namely Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr, and his people. Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 37, verse 140:

﴿When he fled﴾. Ibq (إباق, fleeing as a runaway slave) means fleeing to a place where pursuit cannot find one. So his flight from his people without the permission of his Lord was called "ibaq" (fleeing), figuratively.

﴿To the laden ship﴾, the filled (المشحون, mashhun) one. Yunus, peace be upon him, had promised his people the punishment, but when the punishment was delayed from them, he went out as one hidden from them, headed for the sea, and boarded the ship. It stopped, and they said: "There is a runaway slave here, who has fled from his master." According to what the sailors claim, when there is a runaway aboard a ship, it does not sail. So they cast lots, and the lot fell upon Yunus. He said: "I am the runaway," and he threw himself into the water. This is the meaning of His saying:

**﴿So he drew lots﴾**, he cast lots with them once, or three times, using arrows. Al-musāhamah (casting lots) is the throwing of arrows by way of drawing lots.

**﴿So he was among the losers﴾**, those defeated by the lot.

﴿Then the fish swallowed him﴾, that is, it swallowed him whole,

﴿while he was blameworthy﴾, that is, he had entered into blame.

﴿So had he not been among those who glorify (Allah)﴾: among those who remember Allah much with glorification (tasbih); or among those who say, "There is no god but You; glory be to You; indeed I was among the wrongdoers" (Qur'an 21:87); or among those who pray before that. And it is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: "Every tasbih in the Qur'an is prayer (salah)." It is also said: indeed good deeds raise their doer when he stumbles.

"Had he not been among those who glorify God, he would have remained in its belly until the Day they are resurrected." The apparent meaning is that he remained in it alive until the Day of Resurrection. Qatadah said: "The belly of the fish would have been a grave for him until the Day of Resurrection." He had remained in its belly for three days, or seven, or forty days. And al-Sha'bi said: "It swallowed him at forenoon and spat him out in the evening."

﴿So We cast him onto the open shore﴾, that is, We threw him down onto a bare, empty place where there was no tree and no vegetation,

﴿while he was ailing﴾, weak and sick from what had befallen him from the swallowing of the fish (al-hut). It is related that his body returned to be like the body of a child at the moment it is born.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 37, verse 146:

﴿And We caused a tree to grow over him﴾, i.e., We caused it to grow above him as a shade for him, just as a tent is pitched over a person,

﴿of gourd﴾ (yaqtin). The majority hold that it is the gourd (qar'), and its benefit is that flies do not gather around it, and that it is the fastest of trees in growing, spreading, and rising high. It was said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Indeed, you love the gourd." He said: "Yes, it is the tree of my brother Yunus."

And We sent him to a hundred thousand ﴿وَأرْسَلْناهُ إلى مِائَةِ ألْفٍ﴾. What is meant by this is the people to whom he was sent before the iltiqam (the swallowing by the fish), so "qad" (a particle meaning "indeed" or "already") is understood here as implied.

Or they increase ﴿أوْ يَزِيدُونَ﴾, in the sight of the beholder. That is, when the one who sees them says: they are a hundred thousand, or more.

Al-Zajjaj said: Many have said its meaning is "rather, they increase" (بَلْ يَزِيدُونَ). This is what al-Farra' said, and Abu 'Ubayda, and it is related from Ibn 'Abbas as well.

﴿So they believed﴾, in him and in what he was sent with,

﴿and We let them enjoy [their lives] for a time﴾, until the end of their appointed terms.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 37, verse 149:

﴿So ask them: Has your Lord daughters while they have sons?﴾, is conjoined (ma'tuf) to a similar phrase at the beginning of the surah, namely, "So ask them: Are they stronger in creation?" [al-Saffat: 11], even though the distance between the two has grown long (p-138). He commanded His Messenger to question the Quraysh first about the basis of their denial of the Resurrection, then he continued the speech, connecting some of it to other parts, and then commanded him to question them about the monstrous (dhiza) division they had made, in which they assigned to God (exalted is He) daughters, and to themselves sons, in their saying: "The angels are the daughters of God," together with their intense aversion to daughters, their burying them alive (wa'd), and their disdain for mentioning them.

Verse 37:150: ﴿Or did We create the angels female while they were witnesses?﴾ "Witnesses" means present (حاضِرُونَ). The restriction of their knowledge to direct observation is a mockery of them and a declaration of their ignorance, because just as they did not know this by observation, they did not know it either through God creating knowledge of it in their hearts, nor through a truthful report, nor through a line of reasoning and reflection. Or its meaning is that they say this out of the calm of the soul, owing to the extreme of their ignorance, as if they had witnessed their own creation.

﴿And they have made between Him﴾, between Allah,

﴿Except the sincere servants of Allah﴾ is a disconnected exception (*istithnaʾ munqaṭiʿ*) from *"al-muḥḍarīn"* (those brought forth). Its meaning is: "But the sincere ones are saved from the Fire." ﴿Indeed, you﴾, and they all together,

﴿against Him﴾, against Allah,

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 37, verse 163:

﴿Except those who are destined to burn in the Blazing Fire﴾, with the lām pronounced with a kasra (ṣāli l-jaḥīm). That is: you do not lead astray anyone except the people of the Fire, those who, in His knowledge, had already been decreed to deserve to burn therein because of their evil deeds. It is said: "Fulān tempted (fatana) so-and-so regarding his wife (fatana fulān ʿalā fulān imra'atahu)," just as you say: "he corrupted her for him" (afsadahā ʿalayhi). Al-Ḥasan said: Indeed you, O those who utter this statement, and what you worship of idols, are not, regarding the worship of idols, misleaders of anyone except those who are decreed to roast in the Blazing Fire (yaṣlā al-jaḥīm), that is, to enter the Fire. It was also said: you are not misleaders except those upon whom error was made obligatory in the prior decree. The "mā" in "mā antum" is a negation, and "man" is in the place of the accusative governed by "fātinīn." Al-Ḥasan read "ṣālu l-jaḥīm," with a ḍamma on the lām. Its grammatical basis is that it is a plural; the nūn was dropped for the idafa, and the wāw was dropped because of the meeting of two sukūns, it and the lām in "al-jaḥīm." And "man," is singular in form but plural in meaning, so he took "huwa" according to its form and "al-ṣālūn" according to its meaning.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 37, verse 164:

﴿And there is none of us﴾, [any one of us],

﴿except that he has a known station﴾, [in worship], which he does not exceed. So the modified noun was omitted, and the attribute was put in its place.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 37, verse 165:

﴿And indeed, it is we who are the ranks (al-saffun)﴾. We align our feet in prayer, or we align ourselves around the Throne (al-'Arsh), supplicating for the believers.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 37, verse 166:

﴿And indeed, we are the ones who glorify (Allah)﴾: al-Musabbihun, meaning those who declare Him free of imperfection (al-munazzihun), or those who pray (al-musallun). The more apt reading is that this statement and what precedes it, namely His saying "Glory be to Allah above what they describe" (subhana Allahi 'amma yasifun), is part of the speech of the angels, so that it connects with their mention in His saying: ﴿And the jinn have certainly known﴾ [al-Saffat: 158]. As if it were said: And the angels have certainly known, and they bore witness, that the polytheists are liars against them in regard to the Lord of Might, and they said, "Glory be to Allah," declaring Him free of that, and they excepted the sincere servants of Allah and disassociated them from it, and they said to the disbelievers: "If that is established, then you and your gods cannot seduce anyone of His creation against Allah and lead him astray, except one who is among the people of the Fire." And how could we be fit companions for the Lord of Might, when we are but humble servants before Him? Each of us has a known station of obedience, from which he cannot slip even a fingernail's breadth, out of awe of His greatness. And we are the ones who stand in ranks, setting our feet for His worship, glorifying and extolling Him, as is due from servants to their Lord.

It is also said that it is from the speech of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), meaning: there is not one of the Muslims except that he has a known station on the Day of Resurrection, according to the measure of his deed, from His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿It may be that your Lord will raise you to a praiseworthy station﴾ [al-Isra': 79]. Then he mentioned their deeds, and that they are the ones who form rows in prayer, glorify Allah, and declare Him free of whatever is not fitting for Him.
[Qur'an 37:167] "And indeed they used to say"—that is, the polytheists of Quraysh, before his mission (ﷺ).
"Had we had with us a reminder (dhikr) from the earlier peoples" — that is, a book from the books of the earlier peoples to whom the Torah and the Gospel were revealed.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 37, verse 169:

﴿Had we but been given a Reminder from among those of the former peoples, we would certainly have been the sincerely devoted servants of Allah.﴾ "We would have made our worship purely for Allah, and we would not have denied as they denied, nor opposed as they opposed. Then there came to them the Reminder, which is the master of reminders, and the Book, which is inimitable among the books."

﴿So they disbelieved in it; but they will soon know﴾: the outcome of their denial and the punishment that will befall them. "In" (إنْ) is a lightened form of the heavy "inna" (مُخَفَّفَةٌ مِنَ الثَقِيلَةِ, *mukhaffafa min al-thaqila*, the lightened form of the emphatic particle), and the lam is the distinguishing lam (*al-lam al-fariqa*, the lam that distinguishes it from the negative particle). In that, [it is noted] that they used to say it emphatically, affirming the statement and being earnest about it. How great is the gap between the beginning of their affair and its end!

And We have already decreed Our word to Our servants, the messengers, (Qur'an 37:171).

The "word" (al-kalimah) is His saying:

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 37, verse 172–173:

﴿Indeed, they are the ones who will be given victory﴾ ﴿And indeed, Our soldiers are the ones who will be victorious﴾. He called it a "word" (kalima), though it is "words" (kalimat), because when they were united in a single meaning, they were in the status of a single word (kalima mufrada). What is intended is the promise of their being superior over their enemy in the arena of argument and in the battles of warfare in this world, and their superiority over them in the Hereafter. It is related from al-Hasan: "No prophet was ever defeated in war." And it is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father: "If they are not granted victory in this world, they will be granted victory in the final abode." The summary is that the foundation and basis of their affair, and what predominates in it, is triumph and victory, even though some trial, tribulation, and affliction occur within the course of that, and the lesson is for the predominant outcome.

﴿So turn away from them﴾: that is, disregard them,

﴿for a while﴾: until a brief period, which is the period in which they were given respite; or until the day of Badr; or until the conquest of Makkah.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 37, verse 175:

﴿And see them﴾, i.e., see what will befall them on that Day,

﴿for they will soon see﴾ that. This is for threat, not for distancing. Or: look at them when they are punished, for they will soon see what they denied. Or: inform them, for they will soon know.
﴿Do they then seek to hasten Our punishment?﴾ Before its appointed time.

﴿So when the punishment descends﴾ upon them, [the punishment]

﴿in their courtyard﴾, in their vicinity,

﴿and evil is the morning of those who were warned﴾, their morning. The definite article in "al-mundhirin" (those who were warned) is generic, referring to the category of those who were warned, because "sa'a" (evil is) and "bi'sa" (wretched is) require this [generality]. It has also been said that it refers to the descent of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on the Day of the Conquest (Fath) in Makkah. It is a metaphor for the punishment that descended upon them, after they had been warned and had denied it, by an army whose approach had been announced in advance to their people by one of their well-wishers (nassah), yet they paid no heed to his warning, until it (the army) halted in their courtyard suddenly and launched the raid upon them. It was the habit of their raiders (maghawir) to launch attacks in the morning, so the raid was called "morning" (sabah), even if it occurred at another time.

Translation:

﴿And turn away from them for a time.﴾ ﴿And watch, for they will see.﴾ He repeated it so that it would be a consolation upon a consolation, and an emphasis upon the certainty of the promised reckoning, emphasis upon emphasis. In it there is an additional benefit: the two verbs are left unrestricted by an object, so that it means He sees, and they see, what no mention can encompass, of the various kinds of joy and the types of distress. It was also said: by one of the two is meant the punishment of this world, and by the other the punishment of the Hereafter.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 37, verse 180:

﴿Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of might⁠﴾. The word "Lord" (al-Rabb) is attributed to "might" ('izzah) because it is specific to Him in that respect, as if it were said "the Possessor of might," just as you say "a companion of truthfulness" (ṣāḥib ṣidq), because of its being specific to truthfulness. It is also permissible that what is meant is that there is no might for anyone except that He is its Lord and its Owner, like His saying: ﴿and You give might to whom You will⁠﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 26]. ﴿Above what they describe⁠﴾, namely, of offspring, consort, and partner.

"And peace be upon the messengers" (﴿وَسَلامٌ عَلى المُرْسَلِينَ﴾). He extended the greeting of peace to all the messengers (al-Rusul), after having singled out some of them in the surah, because singling out each one by mention would be lengthy (tatwil).

Qur'anic quotation: ﴿And praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds﴾, for the destruction of the enemies and the victory of the prophets.

The surah included mention of what the polytheists said about Allah and attributed to Him, things from which He is free of, and what the messengers suffered at their hands, and the victory over them that they were promised in the end. So it concluded with comprehensive words of that: the glorifying of His essence above what the polytheists describe Him with, the greeting of peace upon the messengers, and the praise of Allah, Lord of the worlds, for what He ordained for them of good outcomes. The purpose is to teach the believers to say these words, not to neglect them, and not to be heedless of the contents of His noble Book and the deposits of His glorious Qur'an. And from ʿAli (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: "Whoever loves to be measured out with the fullest measure of reward on the Day of Resurrection, let the last of his words when he rises from his assembly be: Glory be to your Lord..." – to the end of the surah.
